sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: State the formula for the area enclosed by a polar curve $r=f(\theta)$ between $\theta=\alpha$ and $\theta=\beta$.
Find the area enclosed by one full loop of $r=3\cos\theta$ (i.e. $\theta\in\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$).
Find the total area enclosed by the cardioid $r=1+\cos\theta$.
Find the area inside the circle $r=3$ but outside the circle $r=2$.
Find the area of one petal of $r=2\sin(2\theta)$, using the interval $\theta\in\left[0,\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ where one petal is traced.
questions.target: Area of one petal of a rose curve

questions.q: Set up (but do not evaluate) the integral for the area inside both $r=2$ and $r=2+2\cos\theta$, noting they intersect where $2=2+2\cos\theta$, i.e. $\theta=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$.
questions.target: Setting up area between curves that intersect
questions.answer: By symmetry, for $\theta\in\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ the circle $r=2$ is the inner (smaller) boundary, while for $\theta\in\left[\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2}\right]$ the cardioid is inner. Area $=\frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}2^2\,d\theta+\frac{1}{2}\int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/2}(2+2\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta$.
questions.explanation: By symmetry, for $\theta\in\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$ the circle $r=2$ is the inner (smaller) boundary, while for $\theta\in\left[\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2}\right]$ the cardioid is inner. Area $=\frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}2^2\,d\theta+\frac{1}{2}\int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/2}(2+2\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta$.

questions.q: Find the total area enclosed by all $4$ petals of $r=3\cos(2\theta)$, using the fact that one petal is traced for $\theta\in\left[-\frac{\pi}{4},\frac{\pi}{4}\right]$.
questions.target: Area of a full rose curve
questions.answer: Area of one petal: $\frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}9\cos^2(2\theta)\,d\theta=\frac{9}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\frac{1+\cos4\theta}{2}\,d\theta=\frac{9}{4}\left[\theta+\frac{\sin4\theta}{4}\right]_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}=\frac{9}{4}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}=\frac{9\pi}{8}$. Total for all $4$ petals: $4\times\frac{9\pi}{8}=\frac{9\pi}{2}$.
questions.explanation: Area of one petal: $\frac{1}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}9\cos^2(2\theta)\,d\theta=\frac{9}{2}\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\frac{1+\cos4\theta}{2}\,d\theta=\frac{9}{4}\left[\theta+\frac{\sin4\theta}{4}\right]_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}=\frac{9}{4}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}=\frac{9\pi}{8}$. Total for all $4$ petals: $4\times\frac{9\pi}{8}=\frac{9\pi}{2}$.

questions.q: Find all points of intersection of $r=2\cos\theta$ and $r=2\sin\theta$ (both circles of radius $1$) by setting the equations equal.
questions.target: Finding intersection points of polar curves
questions.answer: $2\cos\theta=2\sin\theta \Rightarrow \tan\theta=1 \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$ or $\theta=\frac{5\pi}{4}$. At $\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$: $r=2\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\sqrt{2}$. At $\theta=\frac{5\pi}{4}$: $r=2\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{4}\right)=-\sqrt{2}$ (a negative $r$, representing the same point reached differently). Both curves also pass through the pole ($r=0$) at different angles, which must be checked separately.
questions.explanation: $2\cos\theta=2\sin\theta \Rightarrow \tan\theta=1 \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$ or $\theta=\frac{5\pi}{4}$. At $\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$: $r=2\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=\sqrt{2}$. At $\theta=\frac{5\pi}{4}$: $r=2\cos\left(\frac{5\pi}{4}\right)=-\sqrt{2}$ (a negative $r$, representing the same point reached differently). Both curves also pass through the pole ($r=0$) at different angles, which must be checked separately.

questions.q: Explain why checking intersections of two polar curves algebraically (setting $f(\theta)=g(\theta)$) can MISS the pole as an intersection point, and why it must be checked separately.
questions.target: Finding intersection points of polar curves
questions.answer: Different curves can reach the pole ($r=0$) at different values of $\theta$ (since a single point, the origin, corresponds to $r=0$ for ANY $\theta$). Setting $f(\theta)=g(\theta)$ only finds angles where both curves have the SAME $r$ at the SAME $\theta$, so it can miss cases where each curve passes through the origin at a different angle — the pole must always be checked as a separate case.
questions.explanation: Different curves can reach the pole ($r=0$) at different values of $\theta$ (since a single point, the origin, corresponds to $r=0$ for ANY $\theta$). Setting $f(\theta)=g(\theta)$ only finds angles where both curves have the SAME $r$ at the SAME $\theta$, so it can miss cases where each curve passes through the origin at a different angle — the pole must always be checked as a separate case.

questions.q: Explain how the symmetry of $r=3\cos(2\theta)$ about both axes allows the total area to be found by computing just one petal and multiplying, rather than integrating over the full range at once.
questions.target: Area using symmetry to simplify computation
questions.answer: Since $r=3\cos(2\theta)$ produces $4$ congruent petals by symmetry (reflections across both the $x$- and $y$-axes map petals onto each other), computing the area of ONE petal via a single definite integral and multiplying by $4$ avoids having to integrate piecewise across the full $[0,2\pi]$ range while tracking sign changes.
questions.explanation: Since $r=3\cos(2\theta)$ produces $4$ congruent petals by symmetry (reflections across both the $x$- and $y$-axes map petals onto each other), computing the area of ONE petal via a single definite integral and multiplying by $4$ avoids having to integrate piecewise across the full $[0,2\pi]$ range while tracking sign changes.

sections.heading: Part III — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Challenging & Cross-Lesson Synthesis (15–20)

questions.q: Find the area enclosed by $r=\sqrt{\theta}$ for $\theta\in[0,\pi]$ (a spiral arc closed off by the segment back to the pole).
Find the area enclosed by $r=4\sin\theta$ (a circle) for $\theta\in[0,\pi]$, and verify your answer matches the known area formula for a circle of the appropriate radius.
questions.answer: $A=\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\pi}16\sin^2\theta\,d\theta=8\int_0^{\pi}\frac{1-\cos2\theta}{2}\,d\theta=4\left[\theta-\frac{\sin2\theta}{2}\right]_0^{\pi}=4\pi$. This matches $\pi r^2$ for a circle of radius $2$ (since $r=4\sin\theta$ traces a circle of radius $2$ centered at $(0,2)$): $\pi(2)^2=4\pi$ ✓.
questions.explanation: $A=\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{\pi}16\sin^2\theta\,d\theta=8\int_0^{\pi}\frac{1-\cos2\theta}{2}\,d\theta=4\left[\theta-\frac{\sin2\theta}{2}\right]_0^{\pi}=4\pi$. This matches $\pi r^2$ for a circle of radius $2$ (since $r=4\sin\theta$ traces a circle of radius $2$ centered at $(0,2)$): $\pi(2)^2=4\pi$ ✓.

questions.q: Explain why the polar area formula $A=\frac{1}{2}\int r^2\,d\theta$ uses $r^2$ rather than just $r$, by relating it to the area of a thin circular sector.
questions.target: Comparing polar area to rectangular area (conceptual)
questions.answer: A thin sector of angle $d\theta$ and radius $r$ has area approximately $\frac{1}{2}r^2\,d\theta$ (a fraction $\frac{d\theta}{2\pi}$ of the full circle's area $\pi r^2$). Summing (integrating) these thin sector areas over the range of $\theta$ gives the total polar area formula — the $r^2$ arises naturally from the geometry of a circular sector, not from any arbitrary convention.
questions.explanation: A thin sector of angle $d\theta$ and radius $r$ has area approximately $\frac{1}{2}r^2\,d\theta$ (a fraction $\frac{d\theta}{2\pi}$ of the full circle's area $\pi r^2$). Summing (integrating) these thin sector areas over the range of $\theta$ gives the total polar area formula — the $r^2$ arises naturally from the geometry of a circular sector, not from any arbitrary convention.

questions.q: A student claims the area between $r=1$ and $r=2$ (an annulus, full circle) is simply $\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{2\pi}(2-1)^2\,d\theta$. Explain the error and give the correct setup.
questions.target: Comparing polar area to rectangular area (conceptual)
questions.answer: The error is subtracting the radii before squaring — the correct polar formula requires subtracting the SQUARED radii, not squaring the difference of radii. Correct setup: $A=\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{2\pi}\left(2^2-1^2\right)d\theta=\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{2\pi}3\,d\theta=3\pi$ (matching $\pi(2^2-1^2)=3\pi$ from the standard annulus-area formula).
questions.explanation: The error is subtracting the radii before squaring — the correct polar formula requires subtracting the SQUARED radii, not squaring the difference of radii. Correct setup: $A=\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{2\pi}\left(2^2-1^2\right)d\theta=\frac{1}{2}\int_0^{2\pi}3\,d\theta=3\pi$ (matching $\pi(2^2-1^2)=3\pi$ from the standard annulus-area formula).

questions.q: Convert the rectangular point $(0,-3)$ to polar coordinates.
questions.answer: Theorem (Rectangular to Polar Conversion): For rectangular coordinates $(x, y)$, the polar radius and angle satisfy: $r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}, \quad \tan\theta = \frac{y}{x} \mathrm{\ (with\ quadrant\ resolution)}.$ Step 1 · Compute radius $r$: $r = \sqrt{0^2 + (-3)^2} = \sqrt{0 + 9} = \sqrt{9} = 3.$ Step 2 · Determine angle $\theta$: The point $(0, -3)$ lies on the negative $y$-axis. Moving counterclockwise from the positive $x$-axis, the directional angle is $\theta = \frac{3\pi}{2}$ (or $-\frac{\pi}{2}$). Conclusion: In standard polar coordinates with $r > 0$: $\mathbf{\left(3, \frac{3\pi}{2}\right)} \quad \mathrm{or\ equivalently\ } \mathbf{\left(3, -\frac{\pi}{2}\right)}.$
questions.explanation: Theorem (Rectangular to Polar Conversion): For rectangular coordinates $(x, y)$, the polar radius and angle satisfy: $r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}, \quad \tan\theta = \frac{y}{x} \mathrm{\ (with\ quadrant\ resolution)}.$ Step 1 · Compute radius $r$: $r = \sqrt{0^2 + (-3)^2} = \sqrt{0 + 9} = \sqrt{9} = 3.$ Step 2 · Determine angle $\theta$: The point $(0, -3)$ lies on the negative $y$-axis. Moving counterclockwise from the positive $x$-axis, the directional angle is $\theta = \frac{3\pi}{2}$ (or $-\frac{\pi}{2}$). Conclusion: In standard polar coordinates with $r > 0$: $\mathbf{\left(3, \frac{3\pi}{2}\right)} \quad \mathrm{or\ equivalently\ } \mathbf{\left(3, -\frac{\pi}{2}\right)}.$

questions.q: Convert the polar point $(2,\frac{\pi}{2})$ to rectangular coordinates.
questions.target: Area of one petal of a rose curve
questions.answer: Theorem (Polar to Rectangular Conversion): For a point specified in polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$, its Cartesian rectangular coordinates $(x, y)$ are: $x = r\cos\theta, \quad y = r\sin\theta.$ Step 1 · Identify coordinates: Radius: $r = 2$; Angle: $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$. Step 2 · Compute $x$ and $y$: $x = 2\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 2(0) = 0, \quad y = 2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 2(1) = 2.$ Conclusion: The rectangular coordinates are: $\mathbf{(0, 2)}.$
questions.explanation: Theorem (Polar to Rectangular Conversion): For a point specified in polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$, its Cartesian rectangular coordinates $(x, y)$ are: $x = r\cos\theta, \quad y = r\sin\theta.$ Step 1 · Identify coordinates: Radius: $r = 2$; Angle: $\theta = \frac{\pi}{2}$. Step 2 · Compute $x$ and $y$: $x = 2\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 2(0) = 0, \quad y = 2\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = 2(1) = 2.$ Conclusion: The rectangular coordinates are: $\mathbf{(0, 2)}.$

Find the total area enclosed by the curve $r=8+7\sin\theta$.
questions.answer: Expanding $(8+7\sin\theta)^2=8^2+2(8)(7)\sin\theta+7^2\sin^2\theta$ and integrating over $[0,2\pi]$, the linear $\sin\theta$ term vanishes and $\sin^2\theta$ averages to $\frac{1}{2}$, leaving $A=\pi\left(8^2+\frac{7^2}{2}\right)=\frac{177\pi}{2}$.
questions.explanation: Expanding $(8+7\sin\theta)^2=8^2+2(8)(7)\sin\theta+7^2\sin^2\theta$ and integrating over $[0,2\pi]$, the linear $\sin\theta$ term vanishes and $\sin^2\theta$ averages to $\frac{1}{2}$, leaving $A=\pi\left(8^2+\frac{7^2}{2}\right)=\frac{177\pi}{2}$.

questions.q: Find the total area enclosed by the curve $r=5+9\sin\theta$.
questions.answer: Expanding $(5+9\sin\theta)^2=5^2+2(5)(9)\sin\theta+9^2\sin^2\theta$ and integrating over $[0,2\pi]$, the linear $\sin\theta$ term vanishes and $\sin^2\theta$ averages to $\frac{1}{2}$, leaving $A=\pi\left(5^2+\frac{9^2}{2}\right)=\frac{131\pi}{2}$.
questions.explanation: Expanding $(5+9\sin\theta)^2=5^2+2(5)(9)\sin\theta+9^2\sin^2\theta$ and integrating over $[0,2\pi]$, the linear $\sin\theta$ term vanishes and $\sin^2\theta$ averages to $\frac{1}{2}$, leaving $A=\pi\left(5^2+\frac{9^2}{2}\right)=\frac{131\pi}{2}$.

questions.q: Find the total area enclosed by the curve $r=3+5\cos\theta$.
questions.answer: Expanding $(3+5\cos\theta)^2=3^2+2(3)(5)\cos\theta+5^2\cos^2\theta$ and integrating over $[0,2\pi]$, the linear $\cos\theta$ term vanishes and $\cos^2\theta$ averages to $\frac{1}{2}$, leaving $A=\pi\left(3^2+\frac{5^2}{2}\right)=\frac{43\pi}{2}$.

questions.q: Which integral formula calculates the area of a region bounded by the polar curve $r = f(\theta)$ from $\alpha$ to $\beta$?
questions.answer: Polar area is the sum of infinitesimal circular sectors with area $dA = \frac{1}{2} r^2 d\theta$.
questions.explanation: Polar area is the sum of infinitesimal circular sectors with area $dA = \frac{1}{2} r^2 d\theta$.

questions.q: Which integral represents the area inside $r = R(\theta)$ and outside $r = r(\theta)$?
questions.answer: Area is difference of sectors: $\frac{1}{2} \int (R^2 - r^2) d\theta$.
questions.explanation: Area is difference of sectors: $\frac{1}{2} \int (R^2 - r^2) d\theta$.

questions.answer: Outer curve is $6\cos\theta$, inner curve is $3$. Formula: $\frac{1}{2} \int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3} (36\cos^2\theta - 9) d\theta$.

questions.q: Find the area inside both $r = 2$ and $r = 4\sin\theta$ in the first quadrant.
questions.answer: Intersection: $4\sin\theta = 2 \Rightarrow \sin\theta = 1/2 \Rightarrow \theta = \pi/6$. From $0$ to $\pi/6$, bound is $4\sin\theta$; from $\pi/6$ to $\pi/2$, bound is $2$. Sum yields $\frac{4\pi}{3} - \sqrt{3}$.
questions.explanation: Intersection: $4\sin\theta = 2 \Rightarrow \sin\theta = 1/2 \Rightarrow \theta = \pi/6$. From $0$ to $\pi/6$, bound is $4\sin\theta$; from $\pi/6$ to $\pi/2$, bound is $2$. Sum yields $\frac{4\pi}{3} - \sqrt{3}$.

questions.q: What is the range of $\theta$ required to trace the limaçon $r = 2 + \cos\theta$ exactly once?
questions.answer: For a limaçon without loops ($r = a + b\cos\theta$ with $a > b$), the curve is traced exactly once as $\theta$ traverses $[0, 2\pi]$.
questions.explanation: For a limaçon without loops ($r = a + b\cos\theta$ with $a > b$), the curve is traced exactly once as $\theta$ traverses $[0, 2\pi]$.
